title: Saurav Das CJP: Indian government has 'lost the plot' says 'cockroach' party leader after being barred from UK flight
summary:
One of the leaders of India's "cockroach" movement has said the Delhi government has "completely lost the plot" after he was stopped from leaving the country for the UK.
In an interview with the BBC, Das said there were no discrepancies in his documents, accusing the Indian government of using cheap tactics to stop activists from travelling and speaking on issues that matter to young people.
Saurav told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme the incident showed the government was "scared".
"They are scared of the cockroach movement.
"It's a way to harass, to target activists, young voices in India by the Modi government."

summary:

title: Danish top court’s ‘ghetto law’ ruling supports hardline immigration policy
summary:
The country’s top court said eviction of ‘non-Western’ families did not constitute discrimination.
Denmark’s top court has ruled that the eviction of “non-Western” tenants from a social housing estate under the country’s “ghetto law” was not discriminatory.
The country’s “ghetto law” housing legislation, adopted in 2018, allows for the ⁠relocation of residents from areas in which more than half of residents are “non-Western”.
It requires social housing estates to change the social mix by renting at least 60 percent of homes at market rates by 2030.
The 2018 “ghetto law” is aimed at combatting segregation and “parallel societies” in disadvantaged neighbourhoods, according to the government.

title: Number of Students From Crisis-Stricken Countries Rising
summary:
Despite significant declines in overall international student applications and enrollment since the start of the second Trump administration, the number of students in the United States from crisis-stricken countries has increased since 2024, according to a new analysis of international student data.
The growth is likely driven by refugee and displaced students from Nepal, Colombia and Iran, all countries that have recently been devastated by natural disasters or political upheaval.
The report doesn’t include students with temporary protected status; those designated as refugees, asylum seekers or humanitarian parolees; or other displaced students already living in the U.S.
Despite the jump in students from Columbia and Nepal, the countries from which the Trump administration has restricted travel sent far fewer students in 2026.
Laura Wagner, director of refugee student initiatives at the Presidents’ Alliance, said the data reveals how policies such as travel bans affect refugee students.
